title: Obesogen Holdover: Prenatal Exposure Predicts Cardiometabolic Risk Factors in Childhood.
ehr_evidence: The study included nearly 700 mother–child pairs from the Rhea cohort in Greece. The researchers measured concentrations of dichlorodiphenyldichloroethene (DDE), hexachlorobenzene (HCB), and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) in blood samples taken from the mothers around the third or fourth month of pregnancy.
summary: A prospective birth cohort study of nearly 700 mother–child pairs in Crete, Greece, found that higher prenatal exposure to persistent organic pollutants (HCB and DDE) was associated with increased cardiometabolic risk factors and adiposity in children at age 4.
key_findings: A 10-fold increase in mothers' HCB concentrations was associated with higher risks of generalized and abdominal obesity in the children, greater skinfold thickness, higher systolic blood pressure, and a modest increase in child BMI z-score.
Prenatal DDE exposure was associated with higher BMI z-score, increased risk of abdominal obesity, and higher diastolic blood pressure.
PCBs were not associated with any of the cardiometabolic risk factors assessed.
Associations between POPs exposure and cardiometabolic risk factors did not appear to differ between boys and girls.
population: nearly 700 mother–child pairs from the Rhea cohort in Crete, Greece; children assessed at 4 years of age
exposure_domain: persistent organic pollutants (obesogens): DDE, HCB, PCBs
limitations: The study population is relatively small (~700 pairs), and effect modification by sex and long-term health outcomes warrant exploration in larger populations.
